nghe.t: Part 1. You will hear a man telephoning a hotel to book a room. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 10.
Good morning, Harbour View Hotel. Emma speaking. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to book a double room for next month, please.
Certainly. Can I take your name first?
Yes, it's Daniel Kessler.
Is that Kessler with a C or with a K?
With a K. That's K, E, double S, L, E, R.
K, E, double S, L, E, R. Thank you, Mr Kessler. And when would you like to arrive?
On Friday the fifteenth of July. Oh, wait a minute. Sorry, my wife has changed our plans. We're coming a day earlier now, so that's Thursday the fourteenth.
The fourteenth of July. No problem. And how many nights will you stay?
Well, I wanted two nights at first, but we'd like to see a little of the town as well. So let's say three nights, please.
Three nights. So you will leave on Sunday the seventeenth. Can I have a contact number?
Of course. My mobile number is 07911 426 380.
07911 426 380. Lovely. Are you coming on business, Mr Kessler, or is it a holiday?
Neither, really. An old friend from university is getting married in your town, so we're coming for the wedding.

Oh, how nice. A wedding. I'll make a note of that. Now, let me tell you about our rooms. We have two kinds of double room. The standard double is at the back of the hotel. Last year it was sixty-five pounds a night, but the price is now seventy pounds.
Seventy pounds. OK. And what is the room like?
It's quite small, but it's very quiet. I should tell you that it doesn't have a bath. There is a shower, though.
A shower is fine for us. What's the other kind of room?
That's the sea-view double. It's ninety-five pounds a night. Those rooms are on the top floor, and each one has a small balcony, so you can sit outside and look at the harbour.
A balcony! My wife would love that. Let's take the sea-view room.
Good choice. Now, breakfast is not included in the price. It costs eight pounds per person. For children under ten, it's five pounds.
Eight pounds each. That's fine. We haven't got any children with us. One more thing. We're coming by car. Is there anywhere to park?
Yes, we have a free car park for guests. It isn't next to the hotel, though. A lot of people look for it beside the post office, but it's actually behind the bank, on the other side of the street.
Behind the bank. I'll remember that. Thank you very much for your help.
You're welcome, Mr Kessler. We look forward to seeing you in July.

nhom.huongDan: Part 2 — Câu 11–20. nghe.t: Part 2. You will hear a guide giving information to a group of visitors at the entrance of a museum. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 20.
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Castleford Museum. My name is Maria. Before you go in, I'd like to give you some information about the museum and show you where everything is.

First, a little about the building. It is more than a hundred and fifty years old. Because of the tall clock tower, a lot of visitors think that it was once a railway station. In fact, it was built as a factory. Shoes and boots were made here until 1970, and the museum opened ten years later.

Now, some practical things. A ticket still costs six pounds, the same as last year, and guided tours are still only on Saturdays and Sundays. What is different this month is our opening hours. On Fridays, we now stay open until nine in the evening, so you can come after work.

Inside the galleries, please feel free to take photographs. We only ask you not to use a flash. You may also keep your bag with you if it is a small one. What we do not allow in the galleries is food or drink. If you are hungry or thirsty, please use the café.

Where should you begin? Well, most people go straight up to the top floor, because that is where the famous old cars are. Others wait for a tour. My advice is different. Before you do anything else, watch our short film. It is only ten minutes long, and it tells the story of the town. After that, everything else in the museum will make more sense.
Now let me show you where things are on the ground floor. Please look at the plan. We are standing outside the entrance on Museum Street. When you go in, the ticket desk is directly in front of you.

If you have a heavy coat or an umbrella, you can leave it in the cloakroom. That is the first room on your left, just inside the entrance. The gift shop is on the other side, immediately on your right as you go in. People usually visit it at the end, on their way out.

Now, walk past the ticket desk into the main hall. In the middle of the hall, you will see a big steam engine. The cinema room, where the film is shown, is on the left-hand side of the hall, next to the cloakroom. The room opposite the cinema room, on the right-hand side, is the toilets.

At the back of the hall, there are three more places. In the far left corner is the children's activity room, where young visitors can draw and build models. The café is in the opposite corner, on the far right. It has doors that open onto the garden, so in summer you can take your coffee outside.

And finally, to go up to the other floors, you can take the lift. It is in the middle of the back wall, between the children's activity room and the café. Thank you for listening, and enjoy your visit.

nghe.t: Part 3. You will hear two students, Lucy and Sam, talking about the report for their group project on food waste. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 30.
Hi, Lucy. Shall we go through our project report for Dr Patel?
Yes, let's. We should start with the introduction. We have to explain why we chose food waste in the university canteen as our topic.
Right. Did Dr Patel suggest it? I can't remember.

No, he let every group choose freely. And there was very little information about it online, actually. It was my idea, because I have a part-time job in the canteen. Every day I see how much food goes into the bin.
Of course. I'll write that down. Next, the questionnaire. How many students answered it in the end?
Well, we sent it to a hundred and twenty students. After the first week, only sixty had replied.
But then we sent a reminder, didn't we?
Yes, and the final number was eighty-five.
Eighty-five. That's enough for a small study. Now, the results. What was the most interesting thing?
For me, it was the reason why students leave food on their plates. I expected them to say that the food doesn't taste good.
Me too. And I thought they would complain about the prices.
But only a few people said those things. Most students told us that the portions are too big. They simply can't finish their meals.
That was a real surprise. So what should the canteen do? We need to make a suggestion at the end of the report.
Some students wanted lower prices, but that doesn't solve the problem of waste. And I don't think that changing the menu will help.
I agree. What about two sizes of meal, a small one and a large one? Then people can choose how much they want.
Yes, let's suggest that. It's simple, and it's cheap for the canteen.
Good. And when do we have to hand in the report? Is it Monday the tenth?
No, Monday the tenth is the presentation. The report has to be in by Friday the fourteenth.
Oh, good, a few extra days. Can't we have until the twenty-first? Another group told me they had more time.
Dr Patel only gives extra time to students who are ill. So it's the fourteenth for us.
OK. Now, Dr Patel also wants us to write about the problems we had at each stage of the project.
Well, we had a problem right at the beginning, when we were choosing the topic. I wanted food waste, and you wanted to do something about sport.
Yes, and we just couldn't agree. In the end, we had to toss a coin!
And I won. Then we wrote the questionnaire. That didn't take long, and it didn't cost anything, because we put it online.
True, but our first questionnaire had thirty questions. When Dr Patel saw it, he said it was too long, and he told us to cut it to fifteen.
Yes, we had to write it again. After that, we collected the answers. We planned to do that in one week.
And it took three weeks, because people were so slow to reply.
Then I analysed the results. I finished that part on time, but the computer program was so complicated. I had never used it before, and I didn't know how to make a chart.
You should have asked me for help.
I know, but I learned how to do it by myself in the end. And what about the slides for the presentation? You made those.
Don't remind me. My laptop broke on Sunday night, and half of the slides disappeared. I had to make them all over again.
Poor you. Well, at least we have plenty to write about.

cau.giaiThich: Dr Patel KHÔNG gợi ý ("he let every group choose freely" ⇒ loại A); thông tin trên mạng RẤT ÍT ("very little information" ⇒ loại B). "It was my idea, because I have a part-time job in the canteen. Every day I see how much food goes into the bin." ⇒ C.

THE HONEYBEE

The colony

• her job: to lay all the (32) ______
• male bees (drones) do no work and cannot (33) ______
Workers

nghe.t: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about honeybees. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

Good afternoon. In this lecture, I am going to talk about an insect that all of you know, but that few people really understand: the honeybee. I will describe how a colony of bees is organised, how the workers share the jobs in the hive, and how bees make honey.

Let's start with the colony. Honeybees live together in large groups. In the middle of summer, a single colony may contain fifty thousand bees. However, there is only one queen. She is larger than the other bees, and her job is to lay all the eggs. In early summer, she can lay up to two thousand of them every day.

A colony also has some male bees, which are called drones. Drones have an easy life. They do no work in the hive, and they do not collect food. They cannot sting, either, so they cannot protect the colony.

All the other bees are workers, and every worker is female. As the name suggests, the workers do everything. Their lives are short. A worker that is born in summer lives for only about six weeks. A worker born in autumn can live for several months, because she rests inside the hive during the winter.

A worker's job changes as she gets older. A young worker stays inside. Her first job is to clean the hive. She also feeds the baby bees. When she is a little older, she helps to build new cells and to store the food that other workers bring back. Only after about three weeks does she begin to fly outside and look for food herself.

So how is honey made? The workers visit flowers and collect a sweet liquid called nectar. They carry it back to the hive. But nectar is not yet honey. It is about eighty per cent water, so it is very thin. Back in the hive, the bees put the nectar into small cells made of wax. Then they move their wings very fast. This moves the air and dries the nectar. When it is thick enough, the bees close the cell, and the honey is ready. They will eat it during the winter.

Finally, why are bees important to us? It is not only because of honey. When bees fly from flower to flower, they carry pollen from one plant to another. Many plants need this before they can produce food. Without bees, we would have much less fruit. Apples, for example, would be very hard to grow. That is why farmers are worried when their bees become ill. We will look at the reasons for that next week.

nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 1
THE RISE AND FALL OF THE PLASTIC BAG
It was invented to help the planet. So what went wrong?

Go into almost any shop in the world, and your shopping will probably be handed to you in a thin plastic bag. It weighs only a few grams, yet it can carry several kilos of food. It is also extremely cheap to produce. It is no surprise, then, that by some estimates people now use between 500 billion and one trillion plastic bags every year. What is surprising is that this everyday object is only about sixty years old.
The modern plastic bag was created in the early 1960s by a Swedish engineer, Sten Gustaf Thulin. He worked for a packaging company called Celloplast, in the town of Norrköping. Thulin found a way to fold and cut a flat tube of plastic so that it became a strong bag with handles, made from a single piece. The company patented his design in 1965. According to his son, Thulin believed that his invention would be good for the planet. At that time, shops gave their customers paper bags, and making paper meant cutting down trees. A plastic bag was light and strong, and it could be used again and again. Thulin himself always carried a folded bag in his pocket.
For some years, plastic bags were used mainly in Europe. Then, in 1982, two of the largest supermarket companies in the United States began to offer them instead of paper bags, because they cost less. Other shops quickly followed, and within a few years the plastic bag had replaced paper in many countries. Unfortunately, customers did not behave as Thulin had expected. Because the bags were given away free, people saw them as rubbish. A typical bag was used for only about twelve minutes – the time it takes to carry the shopping home – and was then thrown away.
The problems soon became clear. A plastic bag does not break down easily, and scientists think that it may stay in the environment for hundreds of years. Light bags are carried by the wind into trees, rivers and finally the sea. There, turtles sometimes eat them, because a bag floating in the water looks like a jellyfish, which is their natural food. On land, bags cause a different kind of damage. In Bangladesh, plastic bags blocked the drains of the cities, and this made the terrible floods of 1988 and 1998 even worse. In 2002, Bangladesh became the first country in the world to ban thin plastic bags.
Other countries chose a different method. In March 2002, Ireland introduced a tax of 15 cents on every plastic bag. Shops had to charge customers for each bag, and the money was spent on environmental projects. The result was dramatic: within weeks, the number of bags used fell by about 90 per cent. Denmark had in fact taxed bags since 1993, but Ireland's success was the example that many governments decided to follow. Rwanda banned plastic bags completely in 2008, and Kenya did the same in 2017. England waited until 2015 before it introduced a charge of five pence.
Is the answer, then, to go back to paper, or to use cotton bags? It is not so simple. Making a paper bag uses more energy and water than making a plastic one, and paper bags tear easily, so they are rarely used twice. A cotton bag is strong, but growing cotton needs a great deal of land and water. Studies suggest that a cotton bag must be used more than a hundred times before it is better for the environment than a plastic bag. Thick plastic "bags for life" are another choice, but they contain much more plastic than a thin bag, so they are only useful if shoppers really do bring them back to the shop every time.
In the end, the most important thing is not what a bag is made of, but how many times it is used. This is exactly what Sten Gustaf Thulin understood sixty years ago. His son has said that his father would find it very strange that people simply throw the bags away. Perhaps the plastic bag was never the real problem. The real problem is the habit of using something once and then forgetting about it.

READING PASSAGE 2
THE DOCTOR WHO ASKED PEOPLE TO WASH THEIR HANDS
Ignaz Semmelweis found a simple way to save lives – but he could not make other doctors listen

A  Today, everybody knows that washing your hands is one of the simplest ways to stay healthy. Parents teach it to small children, and posters in hospitals remind doctors and nurses to do it before they touch a patient. Yet less than two hundred years ago, most doctors did not wash their hands at all. They often went from one patient to the next in the same dirty coat. The man who first showed that clean hands could save lives was a Hungarian doctor, Ignaz Semmelweis – and for most of his life, almost nobody believed him.
B  Semmelweis was born in 1818 in Buda, which is now part of Budapest. In 1846, he began work as an assistant at the Vienna General Hospital, one of the largest hospitals in Europe. The hospital had two clinics where women could give birth. In the First Clinic, the women were looked after by doctors and medical students. In the Second Clinic, the work was done by midwives – women who are trained to help mothers during a birth. Semmelweis soon noticed something very strange. In the First Clinic, about ten per cent of the mothers died from a fever a few days after their babies were born. In the Second Clinic, the figure was under four per cent. The difference was well known in the city, and some women begged on their knees to be sent to the midwives instead of the doctors.
C  Semmelweis wanted to find the reason. He compared everything in the two clinics: the food, the air, the number of patients, even the position in which the women gave birth. Nothing explained the difference. He even asked the priest of the hospital to stop ringing his bell when he walked through the First Clinic, because he thought that the sound might frighten the women. Then, in 1847, his friend and colleague Jakob Kolletschka died. Kolletschka had been examining a dead body with his students when one of them accidentally cut him with a knife. He quickly developed a fever, and his illness was just like the illness of the mothers. Semmelweis suddenly understood. The doctors and students of the First Clinic often examined dead bodies in the morning and then went straight to the women in the clinic. Something from the bodies was being carried on their hands. The midwives never did this kind of work, so their patients were safer.
D  In May 1847, Semmelweis introduced a new rule. Before entering the clinic, every doctor and student had to wash his hands in a bowl of water mixed with a strong chemical called chlorinated lime. He chose it because it removed the smell of the dead bodies better than soap did. Later, he ordered that the instruments used in the clinic should be washed in the same way. The results came immediately. In April, before the rule, 18 per cent of the mothers in the First Clinic had died. In June, the figure was about two per cent, and in July it was just over one per cent.
E  We might expect that Semmelweis became famous at once. In fact, the opposite happened. Many doctors were angry. They were educated gentlemen, and they did not like the idea that their own hands were killing patients. Besides, nobody at that time knew about germs, so Semmelweis could not explain exactly why his method worked. He did not make things easier for himself, either. He was slow to publish his results – his book did not appear until 1861 – and he wrote rude letters to doctors who disagreed with him, calling them murderers. In 1850, he left Vienna and returned to Hungary. Later, his health became worse, and in 1865 he was taken to a hospital for the mentally ill. He died there two weeks later, at the age of 47.
F  In the 1860s, the French scientist Louis Pasteur showed that tiny living things, called germs, cause many diseases. In Britain, a surgeon called Joseph Lister then used this idea to make operations much safer. At last, doctors could understand why Semmelweis had been right, and hand washing slowly became normal in hospitals. Today, Semmelweis is known as the "saviour of mothers", and a university in Budapest carries his name. Every year on 5 May, the World Health Organization holds a special day to remind health workers to clean their hands. In many hospitals, there is now a bottle of hand gel beside every bed. It is a simple message, but, as the story of Semmelweis shows, simple messages are not always easy to accept.

READING PASSAGE 2
THE DOCTOR WHO ASKED PEOPLE TO WASH THEIR HANDS
Ignaz Semmelweis found a simple way to save lives – but he could not make other doctors listen

A  Today, everybody knows that washing your hands is one of the simplest ways to stay healthy. Parents teach it to small children, and posters in hospitals remind doctors and nurses to do it before they touch a patient. Yet less than two hundred years ago, most doctors did not wash their hands at all. They often went from one patient to the next in the same dirty coat. The man who first showed that clean hands could save lives was a Hungarian doctor, Ignaz Semmelweis – and for most of his life, almost nobody believed him.
B  Semmelweis was born in 1818 in Buda, which is now part of Budapest. In 1846, he began work as an assistant at the Vienna General Hospital, one of the largest hospitals in Europe. The hospital had two clinics where women could give birth. In the First Clinic, the women were looked after by doctors and medical students. In the Second Clinic, the work was done by midwives – women who are trained to help mothers during a birth. Semmelweis soon noticed something very strange. In the First Clinic, about ten per cent of the mothers died from a fever a few days after their babies were born. In the Second Clinic, the figure was under four per cent. The difference was well known in the city, and some women begged on their knees to be sent to the midwives instead of the doctors.
C  Semmelweis wanted to find the reason. He compared everything in the two clinics: the food, the air, the number of patients, even the position in which the women gave birth. Nothing explained the difference. He even asked the priest of the hospital to stop ringing his bell when he walked through the First Clinic, because he thought that the sound might frighten the women. Then, in 1847, his friend and colleague Jakob Kolletschka died. Kolletschka had been examining a dead body with his students when one of them accidentally cut him with a knife. He quickly developed a fever, and his illness was just like the illness of the mothers. Semmelweis suddenly understood. The doctors and students of the First Clinic often examined dead bodies in the morning and then went straight to the women in the clinic. Something from the bodies was being carried on their hands. The midwives never did this kind of work, so their patients were safer.
D  In May 1847, Semmelweis introduced a new rule. Before entering the clinic, every doctor and student had to wash his hands in a bowl of water mixed with a strong chemical called chlorinated lime. He chose it because it removed the smell of the dead bodies better than soap did. Later, he ordered that the instruments used in the clinic should be washed in the same way. The results came immediately. In April, before the rule, 18 per cent of the mothers in the First Clinic had died. In June, the figure was about two per cent, and in July it was just over one per cent.
E  We might expect that Semmelweis became famous at once. In fact, the opposite happened. Many doctors were angry. They were educated gentlemen, and they did not like the idea that their own hands were killing patients. Besides, nobody at that time knew about germs, so Semmelweis could not explain exactly why his method worked. He did not make things easier for himself, either. He was slow to publish his results – his book did not appear until 1861 – and he wrote rude letters to doctors who disagreed with him, calling them murderers. In 1850, he left Vienna and returned to Hungary. Later, his health became worse, and in 1865 he was taken to a hospital for the mentally ill. He died there two weeks later, at the age of 47.

In Britain, a surgeon called Joseph Lister then used this idea to make operations much safer. At last, doctors could understand why Semmelweis had been right, and hand washing slowly became normal in hospitals. Today, Semmelweis is known as the "saviour of mothers", and a university in Budapest carries his name. Every year on 5 May, the World Health Organization holds a special day to remind health workers to clean their hands. In many hospitals, there is now a bottle of hand gel beside every bed. It is a simple message, but, as the story of Semmelweis shows, simple messages are not always easy to accept.

nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 3
SHARING THE BICYCLE
How a failed experiment in Amsterdam became part of city transport all over the world

In many cities around the world, you can now pick up a bicycle on one street, ride it across town and leave it on another. You do not own the bicycle; you simply borrow it for a short time. Bike-sharing schemes like this exist today in about 3,000 cities. They seem like a very modern idea, but the first one was tried sixty years ago – and it was a complete failure.
In the summer of 1965, a group of young people in Amsterdam, who called themselves the Provos, were angry about the growing number of cars in their city. One of them, Luud Schimmelpennink, suggested a simple plan. The group painted some bicycles white and left them in the streets for anyone to use, free of charge. The "White Bicycle Plan" did not last long. The bicycles had no locks, and a city law said that bicycles in the street had to be locked, so the police soon took them away.
Thirty years later, the city of Copenhagen tried again, with a cleverer system. In 1995, it put specially designed bicycles in stands around the city centre. To take one, a user had to put a coin into a lock on the bicycle, in the same way as with a supermarket trolley. When the bicycle was returned to any stand, the coin came back. The bikes were heavy and had solid rubber tyres which could not go flat, and their unusual shape made them easy to recognise. The cost of the scheme was covered by advertisements on the bicycles. However, the coin was worth much less than a bicycle, and nobody knew who was using each bicycle. Many simply disappeared.
The real change came with technology. In 1998, the French city of Rennes introduced a scheme in which users opened the lock with an electronic card. For the first time, the operator knew exactly who had taken each bicycle and when. People who did not bring a bicycle back could be asked to pay for it. In 2005, the city of Lyon used the same idea on a much larger scale, and two years later Paris followed with the most famous scheme of all, Vélib'. It opened in July 2007 with about 7,000 bicycles at 750 stations, and the first thirty minutes of every journey were free for members. In its first year, people made about 20 million trips. There was bad news too: at least 3,000 bikes were stolen in that year, and many more were damaged.
After Paris, cities everywhere wanted a scheme of their own. But stations full of locked bicycles are expensive to build. They also take away space for parking cars, which is not always popular with local shopkeepers. And they have another weakness. In the morning, thousands of people ride into the city centre, so the stations there fill up while stations in the suburbs become empty. In the evening, the opposite can happen. The operators therefore have to pay workers to move bicycles around the city in lorries all day.
Around 2015, companies in China offered a solution: bicycles without stations. Each bike had its own lock, which a user opened with a mobile phone. At the end of the journey, the bicycle could be left almost anywhere. A ride cost very little, and there was no station to look for. The idea spread extremely fast. By 2017, more than 70 companies had put about 16 million of these bikes onto the streets of Chinese cities, and Beijing alone had over two million. It was far more than people needed. Pavements were blocked by carelessly parked bicycles, and when several companies went out of business, millions of unwanted bikes ended up in enormous piles outside the cities.
Since then, cities have learned to control bike sharing more carefully. Many now limit the number of bicycles and mark special parking areas. The newest schemes offer electric bicycles, which make hills and long distances easier, although they cost more to rent. In hilly cities, they have attracted riders who would never have used an ordinary bike. Researchers who have studied bike sharing say that we should be realistic about it. Most trips on shared bikes replace journeys on foot or by public transport, not journeys by car, so the effect on traffic is small. On the other hand, users get more exercise, and a shared bicycle is often the fastest way to travel the last kilometre between a railway station and the office. Sixty years after the white bicycles of Amsterdam, the idea of Schimmelpennink and his friends has finally found its place.

nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 3
SHARING THE BICYCLE
How a failed experiment in Amsterdam became part of city transport all over the world

In many cities around the world, you can now pick up a bicycle on one street, ride it across town and leave it on another. You do not own the bicycle; you simply borrow it for a short time. Bike-sharing schemes like this exist today in about 3,000 cities. They seem like a very modern idea, but the first one was tried sixty years ago – and it was a complete failure.
In the summer of 1965, a group of young people in Amsterdam, who called themselves the Provos, were angry about the growing number of cars in their city. One of them, Luud Schimmelpennink, suggested a simple plan. The group painted some bicycles white and left them in the streets for anyone to use, free of charge. The "White Bicycle Plan" did not last long. The bicycles had no locks, and a city law said that bicycles in the street had to be locked, so the police soon took them away.
Thirty years later, the city of Copenhagen tried again, with a cleverer system. In 1995, it put specially designed bicycles in stands around the city centre. To take one, a user had to put a coin into a lock on the bicycle, in the same way as with a supermarket trolley. When the bicycle was returned to any stand, the coin came back. The bikes were heavy and had solid rubber tyres which could not go flat, and their unusual shape made them easy to recognise. The cost of the scheme was covered by advertisements on the bicycles. However, the coin was worth much less than a bicycle, and nobody knew who was using each bicycle. Many simply disappeared.
The real change came with technology. In 1998, the French city of Rennes introduced a scheme in which users opened the lock with an electronic card. For the first time, the operator knew exactly who had taken each bicycle and when. People who did not bring a bicycle back could be asked to pay for it. In 2005, the city of Lyon used the same idea on a much larger scale, and two years later Paris followed with the most famous scheme of all, Vélib'. It opened in July 2007 with about 7,000 bicycles at 750 stations, and the first thirty minutes of every journey were free for members. In its first year, people made about 20 million trips. There was bad news too: at least 3,000 bikes were stolen in that year, and many more were damaged.
After Paris, cities everywhere wanted a scheme of their own. But stations full of locked bicycles are expensive to build. They also take away space for parking cars, which is not always popular with local shopkeepers. And they have another weakness. In the morning, thousands of people ride into the city centre, so the stations there fill up while stations in the suburbs become empty. In the evening, the opposite can happen. The operators therefore have to pay workers to move bicycles around the city in lorries all day.
Around 2015, companies in China offered a solution: bicycles without stations. Each bike had its own lock, which a user opened with a mobile phone. At the end of the journey, the bicycle could be left almost anywhere. A ride cost very little, and there was no station to look for. The idea spread extremely fast. By 2017, more than 70 companies had put about 16 million of these bikes onto the streets of Chinese cities, and Beijing alone had over two million. It was far more than people needed. Pavements were blocked by carelessly parked bicycles, and when several companies went out of business, millions of unwanted bikes ended up in enormous piles outside the cities.
Since then, cities have learned to control bike sharing more carefully. Many now limit the number of bicycles and mark special parking areas. The newest schemes offer electric bicycles, which make hills and long distances easier, although they cost more to rent. In hilly cities, they have attracted riders who would never have used an ordinary bike. Researchers who have studied bike sharing say that we should be realistic about it. Most trips on shared bikes replace journeys on foot or by public transport, not journeys by car, so the effect on traffic is small. On the other hand, users get more exercise, and a shared bicycle is often the fastest way to travel the last kilometre between a railway station and the office. Sixty years after the white bicycles of Amsterdam, the idea of Schimmelpennink and his friends has finally found its place.
